# Odin 3 Battery Saver

A root-level battery management module for the AYN Odin 3 Ultra (Snapdragon 8
Elite), built on top of DethByte64's [XtremeBS](https://github.com/dethbyte64/xtreme-battery-saver)
engine. It manages CPU cores, background apps, Wi-Fi, Doze mode, and Google
Play Services based on configurable triggers — with no local web server and
no port ever opened on the device. All configuration happens through a plain
text file or a command-line tool.

---

## Table of Contents

- [Overview](#overview)
- [Key Features](#key-features)
- [Compatibility](#compatibility)
- [Installation](#installation)
- [Managing the Module](#managing-the-module)
- [How Configuration Works](#how-configuration-works)
- [Configuration Reference](#configuration-reference)
- [Command-Line Reference (XBSctl)](#command-line-reference-xbsctl)
- [Default Odin 3 Ultra Profile](#default-odin-3-ultra-profile)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)
- [Safety Notice](#safety-notice)
- [Credits & License](#credits--license)

---

## Overview

Odin 3 Battery Saver runs as a lightweight background daemon that reacts to
device state — screen off, charging, low battery, or your own custom
triggers — and applies power-saving actions accordingly. Actions include:

- Disabling or throttling specific CPU cores
- Killing, deprioritizing, or suspending background apps
- Deprioritizing or disabling Google Play Services
- Forcing Android's Doze mode
- Disabling Wi-Fi entirely
- Reporting the device as low-RAM to the OS to reduce background caching

Most settings are safe to experiment with. A few — particularly aggressive
CPU core and process handling — can cause missed notifications, delayed
alarms, or occasional SystemUI instability if pushed too far. Start
conservatively, test one change at a time, and expand from there.

## Key Features

| Capability | Description |
|---|---|
| CPU core control | Disable specific cores, or move them into a `powersave` governor |
| App management | Kill, renice, or suspend third-party apps per event |
| Google Play Services handling | Renice or disable to reduce background battery drain |
| Process-level niceness | Fine-grained priority control over individual system processes |
| Wi-Fi radio control | Fully disable Wi-Fi during selected events |
| Doze mode forcing | Trigger light or deep Doze independent of Android's own timers |
| Event-based configuration | Different behavior for boot, screen-off, charging, low-battery, and custom triggers |
| No local web server | Configuration is file- and CLI-based only — nothing listens on any port |

## Compatibility

- **Device:** Tuned for the AYN Odin 3 Ultra (Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite —
  2 Prime + 6 Performance Oryon cores, no separate efficiency cluster).
  The underlying engine is device-agnostic and works on most rooted Android
  devices, but the shipped default profile assumes this core layout.
- **Root solutions:** Magisk (primary/tested), KernelSU Next. KernelSU and
  APatch are expected to work but are not independently confirmed.

## Installation

1. Flash the zip through Magisk Manager (or your KernelSU/APatch manager) and
   reboot.
2. On first boot, the module writes a default configuration to:
   ```
   /data/local/tmp/XtremeBS/XtremeBS.conf
   ```
   This file is only created if it doesn't already exist, so reinstalling or
   updating the module will never overwrite a configuration you've edited.
3. Edit the config as needed (see below), then either reboot or reload it
   with `XBSctl`.

## Managing the Module

This build has **no WebUI** — there is no local HTTP server, and nothing on
the device listens on any port. Everything is managed through plain files
and a command-line tool:

- Edit `/data/local/tmp/XtremeBS/XtremeBS.conf` with any terminal app (e.g.
  Termux) or root-capable file manager.
- Run `XBSctl` commands from a terminal or via `adb shell`.
- Tapping the module's **Action** button in Magisk Manager prints the
  current status and active configuration to the console — it does not open
  a browser page.

## How Configuration Works

The engine supports two configuration formats:

- **v1** — a flat `key=value` file. Simple, but a single global behavior
  applies at all times.
- **v2** — organized into **event blocks**, allowing different behavior for
  different device states. This is the format used by the shipped default
  configuration and is strongly recommended.

An event block looks like this:

```
event_name={
option=value
option=value
}
```

> The opening `event_name={` and closing `}` must each be on their own line.

Five event names are recognized automatically by the daemon:

| Event | Triggered by |
|---|---|
| `boot` | Device startup |
| `screen_off` | Screen turning off |
| `charging` | Device plugged in and charging |
| `low_power` | Android's built-in Battery Saver being enabled |
| `manual` | Explicitly started/stopped via `XBSctl start` / `XBSctl stop` |

You can also define your own named events (letters, numbers, underscores,
and hyphens only — no spaces, `$`, `=`, `{`, or `}`), which are only ever
applied when you start them yourself:

```
XBSctl start my_event
XBSctl stop my_event
```

Any block may be left empty, in which case that event has no effect. If
multiple active events target the same resource (for example, both
`low_power` and `screen_off` disabling overlapping CPU cores), the settings
combine — a resource stays restricted until every event affecting it has
ended.

## Configuration Reference

| Option | Values | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trigger` | `boot` \| `auto` \| `manual` | `auto` | v1 config only. Ignored in v2 (event blocks replace it). |
| `delay` | integer (seconds) | `3` | Interval between trigger/command checks. |
| `keep_on_charge` | `true` \| `false` | `true` | Keeps power-saving settings active even while charging (v1 `auto` trigger only). |
| `allowlist` | file path | `/data/local/tmp/XtremeBS/apps.allow` | Package names (one per line) exempt from `handle_apps`. Required if using `handle_apps=suspend`. |
| `denylist` | file path | `/data/local/tmp/XtremeBS/apps.deny` | Optional list of system apps to include in `handle_apps` (normally excluded). |
| `handle_apps` | `false` \| `kill` \| `nice` \| `suspend` | `false` | Controls how third-party apps are treated. `suspend` is the most aggressive; `kill` allows apps to restart. |
| `handle_cores` | `false` \| `auto` \| `"cpuN cpuM"` | `false` | Switches selected cores to the `powersave` governor. `auto` detects appropriate cores automatically. |
| `disable_cores` | `false` \| `auto` \| `"cpuN cpuM"` | `false` | Takes selected cores fully offline. `auto` targets the highest-clocked (Prime) cores. |
| `handle_gms` | `false` \| `nice` \| `kill` | `false` | Google Play Services handling. `kill` disables the package entirely — this **will fail SafetyNet/Play Integrity** until reversed. |
| `handle_proc` | `true` \| `false` | `false` | Enables per-process nice-level management via `proc_file`. |
| `proc_file` | file path | `/data/local/tmp/XtremeBS/proc.list` | One process name per line, optionally followed by a nice level (0–19, default 10). |
| `low_ram` | `true` \| `false` | `false` | Reports the device as low-RAM to Android, reducing background caching. |
| `doze` | `false` \| `light` \| `deep` | `false` | Forces Doze mode. May delay notifications/alarms. |
| `kill_wifi` | `true` \| `false` | `false` | Fully disables the Wi-Fi radio (including the Settings toggle) until the event ends. |
| `notify` | `true` \| `false` | `true` | Toggles status notifications when an event changes state. |
| `safemode` | `1` \| `0` | — | Emergency stop. Halts all events until manually resumed via `XBSctl resume`. Persists across reboots until cleared. |

**Nice levels:** range from `-20` (highest priority) to `19` (lowest). Lower
numbers get more CPU time. Unless you have a specific reason to prioritize a
process, avoid negative values.

## Command-Line Reference (XBSctl)

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `XBSctl start [event]` | Starts `manual` (no argument) or a named custom event |
| `XBSctl stop [event]` | Stops `manual` (no argument) or a named custom event |
| `XBSctl pause` | Pauses the daemon's trigger handling |
| `XBSctl resume` | Resumes the daemon, or exits Safe Mode |
| `XBSctl safe` | Immediately stops all events and enters Safe Mode |
| `XBSctl reload` | Reloads the config file (v1 only) |
| `XBSctl status` | Prints current CPU core / Wi-Fi state |
| `XBSctl log` | Prints the configured log file |
| `XBSctl config` | Prints the active configuration file |

If a device becomes unresponsive due to an aggressive configuration, connect
via `adb` from a PC and run:

```
adb shell XBSctl safe
```

## Default Odin 3 Ultra Profile

The configuration shipped with this build is tailored to the Odin 3 Ultra's
Snapdragon 8 Elite, which has two Prime Oryon cores and six Performance
Oryon cores with no separate efficiency cluster.

**Power-saving only applies while the screen is off.** Every other event is
intentionally left empty, so nothing ever restricts performance while
you're actively using the device:

| Event | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `boot` | Intentionally empty — no restrictions at startup. |
| `charging` | Intentionally empty — full performance while plugged in. |
| `screen_off` | The only event that does anything: Prime cores disabled, Performance cores set to powersave, light Doze. |
| `low_power` | Intentionally empty — toggling Android's Battery Saver has no effect. |
| `manual` | Intentionally empty — `XBSctl start manual` does nothing in this build. |

This means battery level, charging state, and Android's own Battery Saver
toggle are all ignored — the single deciding factor is whether the screen
is on. Wi-Fi is left untouched even during `screen_off`, so background
downloads and voice chat aren't interrupted; only CPU cores and Doze are
affected.

Core selection uses `disable_cores=auto` / `handle_cores=auto` rather than
hardcoded core numbers, since the daemon detects the Prime cores directly
from `cpuinfo_max_freq` — more reliable than assuming a fixed core order,
which can vary between kernel builds.

## Troubleshooting

**Device lags, misses notifications, or SystemUI becomes unstable**
Reduce the number of active options and reintroduce them one at a time.
Some Samsung devices are sensitive to CPU core manipulation; some OEMs
behave poorly with `low_ram=true`. If in doubt, disable that option first.

**Is this safe to use?**
Most options carry low risk when introduced gradually and tested. The more
aggressive options (`handle_apps=suspend`, `disable_cores`, `handle_proc`)
have a greater chance of causing missed alerts or temporary instability —
they will not, however, cause a bootloop or hardware damage.

**Do I need to write my own configuration?**
Yes. Every device, workload, and tolerance for background delay is
different — there's no universal "correct" configuration, and copying one
from another device or user is not recommended.

**Can I disable Google Play Services entirely?**
Yes, via `handle_gms=kill`, but this will fail SafetyNet/Play Integrity
checks until the setting is reverted.

## Safety Notice

This module operates with root privileges and can disable radios, CPU
cores, and system services. While it is not expected to cause permanent
damage or hard bootloops, aggressive configurations may cause temporary
instability, delayed notifications, or missed alarms. Test changes
incrementally, keep an allowlist in place before using `handle_apps=suspend`,
and know that `XBSctl safe` (or `adb shell XBSctl safe`) is always available
as an emergency stop.

Use of this software is at your own risk.

## Credits & License

- **Created by:** King Aether
- Built on the original engine and concept by **DethByte64**, [XtremeBS](https://github.com/dethbyte64/xtreme-battery-saver)
- This build: repackaged for the AYN Odin 3 Ultra with the WebUI removed and
  a device-specific default profile. See `CHANGELOG.md` for the full list of
  changes from upstream.
- Licensed under the terms included in `LICENSE`.
